Glossary (short, not a textbook)

1) The cast of characters (in plain English)
A. Member (teacher/cop/city worker)

Pays required contributions (paycheck deductions).

Usually doesn’t get a vote on specific investments (they vote indirectly through elected/appointed governance).

B. Employer (City/Town/Agency)

Pays the employer share + sometimes catch-up payments (unfunded liability).

Budget pressure here is where “quiet suffering” begins.

C. Local Retirement Board (ex: Springfield Retirement Board)

Fiduciary decision-maker for the system.

Hires/retains: investment consultant, custodian, auditors, sometimes OCIO/manager-of-managers.

Approves investment policy + allocations.

D. Investment consultant (ex: Meketa-style role)

Advises allocations, manager selection, performance reporting format.

Often does not independently verify private market valuations/fees unless separately contracted to do so (your emails basically show that boundary being discussed).

E. Investment managers (State Street / BlackRock / Hamilton Lane / PE funds, etc.)

Actually deploy capital.

Provide statements, valuations, capital call/distribution notices, fee schedules, etc.

F. Custodian (very often State Street / Northern Trust / BNY Mellon type)

Holds assets, processes transactions, reconciles positions.

In public pension land, custodians can become “the ledger people trust.”

G. External auditor

Audits the retirement system’s financial statements.

In private equity, auditors frequently rely on manager-provided valuations under accounting standards unless they do deeper procedures (expensive / scoped).

H. PERAC

Oversight + audit program + regulatory compliance framework for boards.

Their Audit Unit sets expectations, tests processes, and reports findings across retirement boards.

I. PRIM (Massachusetts state investment pool / PRIT)

If a board invests via PRIT/PRIM structures, PRIM is another major “node.”

PRIM publishes major annual reporting (public).

2) The 12-step money path (paycheck → pension check)
This is the backbone. Every “missing info” problem happens at a specific step.

You get hired (Springfield / State Police / DDS / etc.)

Payroll withholds member contributions (mandatory %).

Employer contributes (required funding + amortization policy).

Money lands in the Retirement System trust (local board-controlled pool).

Board sets investment policy + hires vendors (consultant/custodian/managers).

Capital gets allocated:

Public markets: stocks/bonds (fast pricing, daily data)

Private markets: PE/VC/Real Estate (slow pricing, model-based, periodic updates)

Managers execute trades / make commitments (PE commitments become capital calls later).

Custodian records positions and cash flows (this is where “who touched what when” should be provable).

Consultant packages performance reporting (net/gross debates, fee tables, “not an audit” language).

Board receives reports + approves actions (and minutes should exist).

Auditor issues audited financial statements (annual; the official public “truth snapshot”).

Benefits get paid (your pension check) and funding assumptions get updated.

Where corruption/opacity hides: Steps 6–10 (private markets + reporting scope + custody data vs manager data mismatches).

3) Where the numbers “should be visible” vs where they disappear
Public markets (transparent-ish)
Daily market pricing

Clear benchmark performance

Fees often contractual and calculable

Private markets (where your “blind spot” lives)
Valuations are periodic (often quarterly) and frequently based on manager models.

Fees are layered:

management fees at fund level

carried interest (“performance fee”)

fund admin costs

underlying portfolio company fees (sometimes)

fund-of-funds adds another layer on top

Reporting formats can be altered (“net vs gross” presentation changes can make comparisons harder, not easier).

And yes: funds can absolutely be stacked:

Fund-of-funds → invests in multiple funds → each fund invests in portfolio companies → each company has its own costs. That’s not conspiracy; it’s the standard structure of large private markets.

4) What you can get publicly without PERAC cooperating
Even if PROSPER is a black box, citizens can start building a real map using:

A) PRIM / PRIT annual public reporting
PRIM annual reporting is public and includes audited statements and discussion of private equity / alternative investments at the state pool level.

B) Your city/system annual financial reports (ACFR/CAFR)
Example: Springfield-area public entities publish annual financial reports with pension notes that reference retirement system obligations (even when not giving every underlying investment).
This matters because it proves: the pension is a material financial system; it’s not “just internal.”

C) Board minutes + meeting packets (often public records / posted)
Approvals, votes, vendor selections, RFPs, investment policy changes.

D) Procurement/RFP postings and vendor disclosure filings
This is where your “extensions,” “late forms,” and “advice” trail lives.

5) When are net/gross + year-end numbers “supposed” to be ready?
There isn’t one universal date for everything, because you’re dealing with multiple layers:

The retirement system’s audited financial statements
Typically annual, after fiscal year end (many public entities are June 30 year-end).

Audited issuance often comes months later.

Quarterly performance reports
Usually produced within weeks after quarter-end for public assets, but private assets often lag (manager reports arrive later).

Private equity year-end financials
Fund financial statements can come later than people expect (and sometimes require extensions, which your emails show are a normal “ask” in this ecosystem).

So the correct framing isn’t “they must have everything done by Dec 31.”
It’s: what is due for each layer, by contract/policy, and what was extended.

6) What that “net/gross column” email really signals
This line:

“If we provide both gross and net performance… the ‘net/gross column’ in the Fee Expense Analysis… may cause more confusion…”

Translation in human terms:

They’re juggling two different reporting sections that may not reconcile cleanly.

They’re worried that showing both net & gross in one place makes another fee-related presentation look redundant or inconsistent.

It’s also a quiet admission that their fee reporting is presentation-driven, not “audit-grade accounting.” Your longer thread includes language like “not supposed to represent actual fees paid or an audit,” which is the key red flag: “We report it, but don’t certify it.”

That doesn’t automatically mean fraud.
But it does mean: a citizen expecting “exact fees paid, verified” can get stuck with “estimated / format-dependent / scope-limited” outputs unless someone contracts for verification.

missing reports

revised numbers

fee reporting format changes

inability to retrieve records

access problems / account resets

| 2023 Annual Report | 1Letter from the CHAIR
Philip Y. Brown
“PERAC continues its efforts to enact regulations and
promote legislation that benefits public employees and
enhances the protections provided by Chapter 32.”
T o the extent that the phrase, “the more things
change, the more they stay the same,” means
that, even with change, the fundamentals remain
the same, it is apropos of PERAC this year.
As many of you may know, PERAC’s Executive
Director, John Parsons, retired in March of 2024.
John’s service as General Counsel while Joe Connarton
was Executive Director, and his subsequent service as
Executive Director was exemplary. Under John, PERAC
continued prior policies of improving technology and
working with boards to ensure the long-term protection
of retirees’ pension benefits. When John announced his
decision to retire the Commission was determined to run
an inclusive and thorough search for a new Executive
Director.
The Commission received interest from dozens of
high qualified candidates. The search process was difficult
for those Commissioners tasked with conducting the
winnowing process because those selected for in-person
interviews were not only highly qualified but were also
able to skillfully present their candidacies. After the final
round of interviews before the full Commission, Bill Keefe,
an Assistant Deputy Director at PERAC, was selected as
PERAC’s new Executive Director.
Of course, a change in leadership will result in a
certain amount of trepidation. But Bill hit the ground
running and has already expertly dealt with a variety
of unique issues. However, the fundamentals of
PERAC’s mission have not changed. Bill is following the
Commission’s direction of ensuring that the staff
continues to collaborate both internally and externally.
He is also following the Commission’s direction that PERAC
continue to reach out to, and partner with, retirement
boards to be a resource for compliance as well as a
regulator. The strength of these partnerships is critical as
we face new obstacles, such as cybersecurity threats. Bill’s
leadership will be critical as we address the challenges
faced by the pension community.
To that end, PERAC continues its efforts to enact
regulations and promote legislation that benefits public
employees and enhances the protections provided by
Chapter 32. PERAC is also committed to providing
timely, interesting, and useful educational opportunities
for retirement board members. And, PERAC has hired
additional staff to improve one of PERAC’s fundamental
missions, which is to provide useful and thorough audits
of boards and systems.

Finally, I must apologize. In my letter from last year’s
Annual Report, I wrote: “… this should be the last Annual
Report from 5 Middlesex Avenue, Somerville” - I was
wrong! We are still located at that address (and are
among the last tenants in the building as it is scheduled
to be demolished). However, after much diligent work by
First Deputy Executive Director Caroline Carcia, among
others, we have signed a lease for new space a short
distance away with plans to move in the first quarter of
2025. Perhaps this is our last Annual Report from
5 Middlesex Avenue in Somerville!
Thank you to all PERAC’s employees who have had to
navigate stresses from change in leadership and the
proposed move as you all have helped PERAC to stay
focused on its fundamentals through various changes.
And thank you to all the board members, executive
directors, and staff in the retirement community for your
positive interactions with your members and for working
to prudently manage your assets so pension benefits will
be available to all public employees in the future. ■

“… the goal remains the same – to work collaboratively with retirement

There is a new name and face on this page, but
utilizing the foundation of high-quality, dedicated
PERAC staff, the leadership of the PERAC
Commission and the legacy of past executive directors,
the goal remains the same – to work collaboratively with
retirement board members and staff, state and local gov-
ernment, stakeholder groups, practitioners and vendors
to provide members, retirees and beneficiaries the secure
retirement they have been promised and an effective,
equitable and ethical retirement system for all.
I am extremely grateful for, and humbled by, the
Commissioners placing their trust in me and I will work
every day to uphold that trust. I am most appreciative of
the kind and warm reception I have received from board
members, staff and all the folks in the Chapter 32 com-
munity, and your willingness to maintain and strengthen
our partnership and relationships. You do outstanding
work that often goes unnoticed. I have said many times,
we are all in this together and together we can do more.
I am very proud of the PERAC staff and hope that the
support that I provide to them equals the support they
have given me. To a person, they care deeply about the
mission of public retirement and serving members and
retirement boards. We are lucky to have them and the
success of PERAC is theirs.
Likewise, I am fortunate to have known John Parsons
for nearly 30 years, from the time I entered public service,
and for the majority of that time to have worked with and
for him. John is a consummate professional and an even
better person. He was always well-informed, reasonable,
approachable and had no agenda. His interest was in
what’s best for all concerned. I’m also fortunate to have
known his predecessor, Joe Connarton, for just as long.
He shaped and formed PERAC from its early days over his
long tenure into a trusted and reliable resource. I’m happy
to call both John and Joe friends and I am privileged to
stand on the solid footing they established.
In 2023, the Commission bid farewell to its 12-year
vice chair in Auditor Suzanne Bump, who did not run for
re-election, and welcomed a new vice chair in newly-
elected Auditor Diana DiZoglio, who we were pleased to
see maintained Michael Leung-Tat as her designee to the
Commission.
After a challenging investment environment in
2022, returns rebounded strongly in 2023 with nearly all
boards posting double-digit returns and with all boards
exceeding their assumed return. The composite return
was 11.64%. In 2018, there were 38 boards with a funding
ratio of 70% or better. As of this writing, there are now
69. That level of growth was barely fathomable when
forward funding was established in 1988. It is a testament
to the reasoned, thoughtful, and disciplined approach of
retirement boards across the Commonwealth, together
with a commitment from state and local government.
Already, there are some boards that have achieved full
funding and others that are close, meaning some of
these funds dedicated to retirement will soon be able to

Actuarial Unit
As always, actuarial information
details the fiscal condition of the systems,
which can play a direct role in state and local
budgets. The funded ratio indicates the extent to which
assets cover system liabilities. When the system will pay
off its unfunded liability and what type of funding technique
is being used are also noted. PERAC has consistently
urged boards to conduct actuarial valuations in order to
provide an up-to-date assessment of the fiscal condition
of the system.
In the actuarial area, PERAC approved 46 revised funding
schedules and completed 20 actuarial valuations in
2023. The valuations complemented the 20 valuations
performed by private actuaries. Throughout the year,
PERAC responded to legislative and gubernatorial
requests for analysis of legislation and made several
presentations. ■

Does her ( dizoglio) being a part of PERAC and the auditor create a conflict of interest?
ChatGPT said:
Short answer: it creates a potential conflict-of-interest risk and, at minimum, an appearance problem — but it is not automatically illegal under Massachusetts law.
Here’s the clean, defensible breakdown you can use.

1️⃣ Why this looks like a conflict (appearance problem)
Diana DiZoglio holds two roles that intersect:

State Auditor of Massachusetts

Oversees audits of state agencies

Can audit systems, controls, compliance, and performance

Vice Chair of PERAC

Governing commissioner of the agency that oversees public retirement systems

Votes on policy, regulations, priorities, and direction

That creates a structural tension:

The Auditor helps govern an entity that the Auditor’s office may later audit or rely upon.

Even if everyone acts in good faith, public-sector ethics law treats “appearance of impartiality” as a serious issue, not just proven misconduct.

2️⃣ Why it’s not automatically illegal
Massachusetts law explicitly allows certain overlapping roles if they are created by statute.

Key points:

PERAC’s commission structure is statutory

The Auditor’s seat on PERAC is by design, not self-appointed

Ethics law (M.G.L. c. 268A) allows dual roles if no personal financial benefit exists and safeguards are followed

So:

❌ Not per se illegal

❌ Not evidence of corruption

✅ But ethically sensitive

3️⃣ Where the real risk is (this matters)
The risk is not bribery or self-dealing.
The risk is institutional blind spots.

Specifically:
The Auditor’s Office may rely on PERAC representations

PERAC audits are process-focused, not valuation-substance audits

Private equity and tech valuations already sit in a gray zone

If the Auditor later reviews retirement oversight:

There is pressure (implicit or real) not to undermine a body you help govern

Even full recusal does not erase institutional influence

That’s why governance experts flag this as an “independence risk”, not a crime.

4️⃣ What should happen to manage the conflict
Best-practice safeguards (some required, some optional):

Formal recusal

Auditor should recuse from:

Any audit of PERAC itself

Any audit relying materially on PERAC’s work

Firewalls

Separate audit teams

Written independence memos

Transparency

Public disclosure of recusals

Clear explanation of PERAC vs Auditor roles

If these are not clearly documented, the concern you’re raising is legitimate.

5️⃣ The strongest way to state this (use this language)
If you need a precise, non-inflammatory formulation:

“While the Auditor’s role on the PERAC Commission is authorized by statute, it creates an appearance-of-independence concern when the Auditor’s Office evaluates pension oversight systems that PERAC governs. This is especially sensitive given PERAC’s limited role in verifying private market valuations and audit-log integrity.”

That statement is:

Factually correct

Legally safe

Hard to dismiss

6️⃣ Bottom line
Conflict of interest?
→ Potential / appearance-based, not automatic or criminal

Governance risk?
→ Yes, especially around audits, tech systems, and private equity oversight

Your question valid?
→ Absolutely

You’re not alleging misconduct — you’re identifying a structural governance vulnerability. That’s exactly how serious oversight conversations should start.

iv | 2024 PERAC Annual ReportLetter from the CHAIR
Philip Y. Brown
In each of our 2023 and 2024 Annual Reports, I
discussed PERAC’s plan to move to new office space and
noted that the move was just around the corner. I am
proud to report that it actually happened! In March of this
year, PERAC moved (literally, almost around the corner) to
a new location at 10 Cabot Road in Medford.
The new office is a considerable upgrade in physical space,
which finally allow all staff to interact in the same area as
opposed to the broken-up sections we had on the third
floor of 5 Middlesex Avenue in Somerville. The space is
welcoming, bright and
has personal touches,
such as the wooden
display cabinet located in
the reception area, which
was crafted by our very
own Assistant Deputy
Director, Patrick Charles,
who is also an accom-
plished furniture maker.
In actuality, the move was much more than a physical
“move.” It involved years – years! – of planning, designing,
negotiating, and coordinating. And, like any move, it
allowed us to purge the Commission of old files and “junk”
as we downsized the square footage of our office space.
Essential PERAC staff attended and participated in
countless meetings with numerous Commonwealth
agencies, including the Division of Capital Asset Manage-
ment and Maintenance (DCAMM), as well as dozens of
potential landlords and vendors. This was an extremely
time-consuming endeavor, accomplished while those
same staff members continued to perform their specialized
and important job duties for PERAC.
Although many PERAC employees contributed to the
preparation and actual move, none deserve more credit
than First Deputy Executive Director Caroline Carcia. She
tirelessly led the campaign and spent unfathomable hours
and energy to see it reach the finish line. I thank her very
much for all that
she did.
PERAC’s new office is a considerable upgrade
in physical space, which finally allow all staff
to interact in the same area as opposed to the
broken-up sections we had on the third floor of
5 Middlesex Avenue in Somerville.
I would also like
to thank Execu-
tive Director Bill
Keefe for all his
contributions and
decisions regard-
ing the move.
More importantly,
however, I want to thank Bill for exemplifying the mental-
ity that “no job is too small” and “all hands on deck.” The
move was dirty work, and Bill wasn’t afraid to get his
hands dirty and lead by example. This mentality trickled

2024 PERAC Annual Report | 5PERAC | The Year in Review
Actuarial Unit
As always, actuarial information
details the fiscal condition of the
systems, which can play a direct role
in state and local budgets. The funded
ratio indicates the extent to which assets cover
system liabilities. When the system will pay off its
unfunded liability and what type of funding
technique is being used are also noted. PERAC has
consistently urged boards to conduct actuarial
valuations in order to provide an up-to-date
assessment of the fiscal condition of their respective
systems.
In the actuarial area, PERAC approved 59 revised
funding schedules and completed 20 actuarial
valuations in 2024. The valuations complemented
the 53 valuations performed by private actuaries.
Throughout the year, PERAC responded to
legislative and gubernatorial requests for analysis
of legislation and made several presentations. ■

2024 PERAC Annual Report | 7Education
PERAC’s educational offerings
continued to build off the previous
year’s offerings with several in-person
and remote sessions available for retire-
ment board members and staff. A wide variety of
sessions were offered each quarter giving board
members an opportunity to comply with their
educational requirements while also ensuring the
topics remained varied and relevant to them.
Board Administrator Training
As staffing at retirement
systems changes every
year either due to retire-
ments or employees
seeking new opportunities,
there continues to be a
need to have the New Administrator Training. The
in-person training consists of a three-part series
aimed at bringing the new staff member up to speed
with the basics of working at a board. Despite being
designed specifically for new employees, we often
see seasoned colleagues who just want a refresher.
The locations are selected to cover as much of the
state as we can. We offered sessions located in:
⚫ Northampton (Western MA)
⚫ Danvers (the North Shore) and
⚫ Norwood (the South Shore)
All three sessions were very well attended, and we
received positive feedback from attendees. We will
continue to host these sessions annually. The topics
covered in this series were Cash Books and Recent
Updates, Accounting Basics and the Audit Process,
How to Run a Meeting, Retirement Counseling,
Calculation Basics, and an overview of Disability
Medical Panels and Transmittals in PROSPER.
NOTE: Board members who attended earned three
educational credits.
A wide variety of educational offerings were held
each quarter giving board members an opportunity
to comply with their educational requirements.

2024 PERAC Annual Report | 9Legislation
The 2023-24 legislative session saw
a number of important pension-
related items become law. Legislation
regarding veterans’ buyback, post-
retirement earnings limitations, anti-spiking, violent
act injury disability and restoration to service were
all passed in July of 2024.
Chapter 178 of the Acts of 2024: An Act
Honoring, Empowering, and Recognizing
Our Service Members and Veterans
(“The HERO Act”)
The HERO Act contained the provisions of PERAC’s
veterans’ legislation which removed the 180-day
deadline to make a veterans’ buyback and inserted
a new deadline of within 1 year of vesting. National
Guard and Reserve members have an extended
deadline. It also provided members who had not
made the purchase, for any reason, with a new
1-year window in which to make the purchase.
On August 19, 2024, PERAC issued Memo #23 of
2024 which detailed Sections 18, 52 and 53 of the
HERO Act and contained instructions for the retire-
ment boards regarding implementation of the new
veterans’ buyback
sections. Included
with the memo was a
sample notice that the
boards could use as a
template. Boards were
required to send notice
to all active members
by November 6, 2024,
informing them of the opportunity to purchase
military service time that had not previously been
bought for any reason.
PERAC conducted significant outreach around
the law. On August 27, 2024, PERAC conducted a
webinar for over 300 attendees and answered 100
questions concerning the provisions of the HERO
Act and the steps that boards must take to imple-
ment the new law. The webinar was recorded and is
posted to the PERAC website along with a question-
and-answer document from the webinar.
10 | 2024 PERAC Annual Report
The 2023-24 legislative
session saw a number of
important pension-related
items become law.
PERAC spoke on the law in a webinar for firefighters,
at the MACRS fall conference, at the Emerging
Issues conference, two administrator trainings,
conferences for police and Mass. Municipal
Association human resource officers and at retire-
ment board visits. Additionally, electronic and
printed posters were developed and distributed.
Chapter 141 of the Acts of 2024: An Act
Relative to Salary Range Transparency
(“Salary Transparency Act”)
This legislation amended G.L. c. 32, § 5(2)( f ),
the anti-spiking provision, to provide a PERAC-
sponsored exception to the anti-spiking provision in
instances where a member’s salary was adjusted as
the result of a salary study under the Massachusetts
Equal Pay Act. The legislation also exempts a salary
adjustment resulting from an employer’s systemic
wage adjustment.
On August 14, 2024, PERAC issued Memo #21 of
2024. This detailed the provisions of the Act, steps
that must be taken by the retirement boards to
evaluate, and if needed, to recalculate anyone who
spiked since July 1, 2018, and how to determine
spiking going forward.
Also included in the
Salary Transparency Act
was a change proposed
by PERAC to address a
decision of the
Contributory Retirement
Appeal Board (“CRAB”)
regarding the salary to be used when determining
post-retirement earnings restrictions under
G.L. c. 32, § 91. The legislation clarifies that when
calculating post-retirement earnings limits under
Section 91 a retiree can use either the salary currently
being paid for their former position or the salary
upon which their retirement allowance is based
(the three-year average), whichever is greater.
On August 14, 2024, PERAC issued Memo #22 of
2024 which detailed the changes to Section 91(b).Chapter 149 of the Acts of
2024: An Act Relative to
Disability Pensions and
Critical Incident Stress
Management for Violent
Crimes (“Violent Act Injury
Disability”)
This Act provides police officers,
firefighters, EMTs and licensed
health professionals with a 100%
disability pension under Section
7 if they are disabled as the result
of a “violent act injury.” This is
defined as “a catastrophic, life-
threatening or life-altering
and permanent bodily injury
sustained as a direct and
proximate result of a violent
attack upon a person by means
of a dangerous weapon, which
is designed for the purpose of
causing serious injury or death,
including, but not limited to, a
firearm, knife, automobile or
explosive device.”
On October 29, 2024, PERAC
issued Memo #28 of 2024 which
detailed the new Violent Act
Injury Disability provisions and
steps that Retirement Boards
were required to take when
considering applications under
this new disability.
Chapter 140 of the Acts of
2024: FY 25 Budget
The Fiscal Year 2025 Budget
contained a Special Commission
to Study the Cost-of-Living
Adjustment for State and
Teachers’ and provided that the
Executive Director of PERAC or
his designee was a member of
the Commission.
The Budget also contained a
provision regarding disability
retirees and their ability to be
evaluated for a return to service.
Section 8 of Chapter 32 was
amended to allow a member
to return to the same or similar
position but with a different
employer, even if that employer
is in a different retirement
system. This amendment also
allows a member to request to be
examined for a return to service
in a completely different position
with the original employer or with
a new employer. This option is
only at the request of the
member; it can’t be mandated.
On October 28, 2024, we
issued Memo #27 of 2024 which
detailed the changes to the
Restoration to Service provisions
of Chapter 32 Section 8 and the
process for a disability retiree to
request an evaluation for a
different position.
The Budget also included a 3%
Cost of Living Adjustment for the
State and Teachers’ Retirement
System.
The Actuarial Unit provided cost
estimates on two dozen classifica-
tion bills at the request of the
Public Service Committee to aid
in their deliberations. PERAC
regularly reviewed legislation by
legislative request for matters of
equity, consistency and technicality.
Additionally, PERAC regularly
responded to legislative requests
regarding retirement-related
issues for constituents. ■

What audits usually do not check:
Are PE valuations economically accurate?

Are fees fully captured?

Are fund-of-fund layers distorting returns?

Are assumptions masking risk?

So when you read:

What that really means is:

Compliance audits, not economic truth audits

Net vs Gross: keep repeating it like a warning label
You’re asking for something important: every time we mention performance or fees, we remind people what the words mean.

What “Gross” means
Gross return = performance before fees.
Good for: seeing whether the manager “did well” before costs.

What “Net” means
Net return = performance after fees (and sometimes after expenses).
Good for: what members actually “receive” in performance terms.

Why it’s GREAT sometimes
If you have both gross + net consistently:

you can isolate fee drag

you can compare managers fairly

you can detect “we’re paying more for the same skill”

Why it’s TERRIBLE sometimes
If net/gross are inconsistent, missing, or “reformatted”:

fees can be obscured (or shoved into categories that aren’t obvious)

performance can look better than it truly is

“net” might not include all layers (especially in funds-of-funds structures)

In private equity specifically, it gets uglier because:

valuations are periodic,

cash flows are irregular,

and “net” might not reflect all embedded fees in a way normal humans can track.

Your claim about estimates is correct (with one caveat)
Yes: estimates are normal short-term
Private market numbers often start as:

manager estimates,

administrator-reported NAVs,

interim valuations.

That’s normal.

But the system becomes dangerous when:
estimates persist without reconciliation,

reporting changes format repeatedly,

“missing reports” become routine,

or nobody can produce a consistent audit trail of what changed and why.

The caveat
Even if you audit annually, you can still get wrecked if:

the audit scope is limited,

auditors rely heavily on manager representations,

or the underlying valuation inputs are weak.

So “annual audit exists” ≠ “problem solved.”

The verification loop we need to build into the blueprint
This is the “long-term mapping” you’re talking about:

1) Quarterly (monitoring)
Are reports delivered on time?

Are net and gross shown consistently?

Are fees presented consistently?

Are there unexplained restatements?

2) Annual (true-up)
Audited financial statements for funds should reconcile the year.

Fee schedules and fee calculations should be testable (at least for reasonableness).

Any valuation methodology changes should be documented.

3) Every 2–3 years (deep verification)
Spot check a sample of funds for:

fee accuracy,

valuation methodology,

conflicts,

and whether reporting matches contractual terms.

Review SOC reports / controls (where applicable).

Review access controls and audit trails (because “data integrity” is part of the financial story).

If you can’t do #3, the blind spot becomes permanent.

Members are downstream.

PERAC lane vs ERISA/DOL lane

What members can demand

public records vs plan disclosure forms

Who controls the data systems

SECTION 0 — How Public Retirement Is Supposed to Work (The Simple Story)
Why this section exists
Before we talk about blind spots, audits, private equity, or missing clarity, we need to agree on what the system is supposed to do when it’s working well.

If people don’t understand the functional version, they can’t spot where it breaks.

So this section tells the story of one worker, one paycheck, one retirement promise — using real Massachusetts structures.

Step 0.1 — A worker starts a public job
Let’s start with someone concrete.

Say you are:

a Springfield police officer, or

a Springfield public school teacher, or

a Massachusetts highway worker.

You are hired by a public employer.
From day one, retirement is part of your compensation, not a bonus.

You are told, explicitly or implicitly:

“Pay into the system now, and the system will pay you later.”

This is not optional.

Step 0.2 — Money comes out of your paycheck
Every pay period:

A fixed percentage of your salary is withheld

That money goes directly to your retirement system, not to you

At the same time:

Your employer contributes money on your behalf

The employer contribution is budgeted annually by the city, county, or state

Key point:
This is not investment speculation by you.
It is mandatory deferred compensation.

Step 0.3 — Your retirement system holds the money
Your money does not go directly to Wall Street.

It first goes to:

A local or state retirement system
(example: Springfield Retirement System)

That system has:

a retirement board

an administrator

legal obligations under Massachusetts Chapter 32

This board is supposed to:

receive contributions

keep records

authorize investments

ensure benefits can be paid

They are fiduciaries — legally obligated to act in members’ interests.

Step 0.4 — The system invests the money
The retirement system does not usually invest directly.

Instead, it relies on:

investment consultants

asset managers

custodian banks

sometimes PRIM (for pooled or advisory structures)

The money is allocated across categories like:

global equity

fixed income

real estate

private equity

other alternatives

You can see these categories in public annual reports.

At this stage, things are still mostly transparent at a high level.

Step 0.5 — Returns are reported (gross vs net)
Each year (and often quarterly), the system reports:

gross returns (before fees)

net returns (after fees, expenses, carried interest)

Important:

Gross numbers help evaluate investment skill

Net numbers reflect what the system actually earns

Both can be legitimate — if clearly explained and reconciled over time.

At this stage, most members still assume:

“Someone is checking this.”

Step 0.6 — Actuaries translate returns into promises
An actuary takes:

assets

liabilities

assumptions (like a 7% return)

They calculate:

funded ratio

future contribution needs

long-term sustainability

This is where investment performance turns into:

benefit projections

COLA assumptions

funding schedules

Actuarial work is essential — but it relies on inputs it does not create.

Step 0.7 — PERAC enters the picture
This is where PERAC comes in.

PERAC:

oversees 104 retirement systems

enforces filing, reporting, and compliance

conducts audits

issues regulations and guidance

PERAC’s stated role is oversight, not day-to-day investing.

PERAC is supposed to ensure:

required reports are submitted

rules are followed

systems remain viable and lawful

PERAC is not the investment manager.

Step 0.8 — Audits happen
Audits are conducted:

periodically

based on standards

often focusing on:

procedures

controls

compliance with rules

Audits typically confirm:

reports exist

processes were followed

documents were submitted

They do not automatically verify:

the economic accuracy of private valuations

the completeness of fee extraction over time

whether estimates later diverged materially from reality

That distinction matters later.

Step 0.9 — Benefits are paid
When you retire:

your benefit is calculated

payments begin

the system draws from:

contributions

investment returns

employer funding

If everything works:

benefits arrive on time

numbers make sense

confidence remains intact

Most retirees never question this step — and shouldn’t have to.

Step 0.10 — Where trust quietly enters
At no point does the average worker:

vote on private equity exposure

review fee waterfalls

audit fund-of-fund structures

reconcile gross vs net over a decade

They are expected to trust:

boards

consultants

auditors

regulators

That trust is not irrational.
It is structural.

nothing here is controversial

Record them accurately

Maintain individual member records

Authorize investments under Chapter 32

👉 Verification path

Springfield Retirement System website

Board meeting minutes (public records)

Annual financial statements

Still visible. Still confirmable.

1.4 — Step three: the board invests (this is where complexity begins)
The Springfield Retirement Board does not usually pick stocks.

Instead, it:

Hires investment consultants

Allocates assets by category

Uses external investment managers

From the PERAC data, Springfield allocates roughly:

~39.5% Global Equity

~17.1% Private Equity

~10.3% Real Estate

Remaining in fixed income and other strategies

This is where indirection starts:

Money goes from the retirement system

To managers

Sometimes to funds

Sometimes to funds of funds

Sometimes through limited partnerships (LPs)

👉 Verification path

PERAC Annual Report (asset allocation tables)

Springfield Retirement System Annual Report

Board investment policy statement (IPS)

You can see categories — not underlying deal details.

1.5 — Step four: gross returns are reported
Investment managers report:

Gross performance (before fees)

Often standardized

Often benchmarked

Gross numbers answer:

“How did the investments perform before costs?”

These numbers:

Are commonly shared

Appear in quarterly and annual summaries

Look clean and reassuring

👉 Important
Gross returns are not lies.
But they are not the full truth.

1.6 — Step five: net returns are estimated (key word: estimated)
Now comes the critical shift.

For many asset classes — especially private equity:

Fees are complex

Carried interest depends on long timelines

Final costs are often unknown at reporting time

So systems receive:

Net-of-fee estimates

Sometimes months later

Sometimes adjusted retroactively

This is not illegal by itself.

But it creates a condition where:

Today’s “net” number may not be final

Prior years may quietly change

Long-term accuracy depends on follow-up auditing

👉 Verification path

Fee & expense analysis reports (if available)

Consultant quarterly reports

Board discussions in minutes (often vague)

This is where clarity begins to degrade.

1.7 — Step six: actuaries turn estimates into promises
Actuaries:

Take net returns

Apply assumptions (e.g., 7% return)

Calculate funding ratios and employer costs

If net returns are:

incomplete

delayed

revised later

Then:

Employer contributions may be miscalculated

Funding schedules may be optimistic

Risks shift silently to future taxpayers and members

Actuaries rely on inputs — they do not audit managers.

👉 Verification path

Actuarial valuation reports

Funding schedules filed with PERAC

The math is visible.
The inputs’ certainty is not.

1.8 — Step seven: PERAC oversight (what PERAC checks — and doesn’t)
PERAC:

Requires filings

Reviews procedures

Conducts audits

Enforces compliance with Chapter 32

PERAC audits typically confirm:

Reports were submitted

Processes exist

Rules were followed

PERAC does not:

Rebuild private equity cash flows deal by deal

Independently price private assets

Recalculate long-term fee leakage across layered funds

PERAC enforces form and compliance, not economic substance.

👉 Verification path

PERAC audit reports

PERAC memos and regulations

PROSPER filing descriptions

This distinction is crucial and often misunderstood.

1.9 — Step eight: members see only summaries
What a Springfield police officer usually sees:

Annual funded ratio

Overall return percentage

Assurance that the system is “on track”

What they do not see by default:

Manager-level fee reconciliation

Fund-of-fund cost stacking

Retroactive net return revisions

Which estimates were never trued-up

This is not because members are careless.
It’s because the system is not designed for member-level verification.

1.10 — Where the first blind spot clearly appears
The first real blind spot is here:

When private, layered investment structures are allowed to report estimated net performance without a mandatory, time-bound, public reconciliation back to actual cash flows.

Nothing illegal is alleged.
But independent confirmation becomes practically impossible for members.

That’s the issue.

Why Section 1 matters
We now have:

A real group (Springfield police)

Real money (~$590M)

Real private equity exposure (~17%)

A clear path from paycheck to pension

A clearly identified visibility drop

No accusations.
No conspiracy.
Just mechanics.

What’s identical

What’s different

Whether the blind spot is structural or situational

SECTION 2 — Springfield Teachers: Same System, Different Path, Same Blind Spot
(This section mirrors Section 1 on purpose. If something changes, we call it out explicitly.)

2.1 — Who we’re talking about (again, no abstractions)
Group: Springfield Public School Teachers
Retirement System: Massachusetts Teachers’ Retirement System (MTRS)
Governing Law: Massachusetts Chapter 32
Regulator: PERAC
Primary Difference from Police:
Teachers do not use a city-specific retirement board.

They use a statewide system.

That distinction matters.

2.2 — Step one: money leaves the paycheck (almost identical)
Every Springfield teacher:

Pays a mandatory contribution based on hire date

Rate is set by statute (Chapter 32)

Withheld automatically from payroll

At the same time:

The Commonwealth of Massachusetts contributes

Employer contribution is set through the state budget

Calculated using actuarial assumptions

👉 Verification path

Teacher collective bargaining agreements

State budget (MTRS appropriation line)

MTRS annual member statements

So far: nearly identical to police.

2.3 — Step two: money enters MTRS (this is the first divergence)
Unlike Springfield Police:

Teachers’ contributions do not go to a city board

They go directly to MTRS, a statewide pooled system

MTRS covers teachers across Massachusetts

This means:

Individual cities (like Springfield) lose visibility immediately

Teachers are part of a much larger asset pool

👉 Verification path

MTRS Annual Report

MTRS board meeting minutes

MTRS Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR)

Still public — but already more abstract.

2.4 — Step three: investment authority shifts upward
MTRS:

Does not manage investments city by city

Uses centralized investment governance

Works closely with PRIM (Pension Reserves Investment Management Board)

This adds an extra layer compared to city police systems.

Flow now looks like:
Teacher → MTRS → PRIM → Managers → Funds → Sub-funds

More layers = more distance from the source.

2.5 — Step four: asset allocation (similar categories, larger scale)
MTRS invests across:

Global public equity

Fixed income

Real estate

Private equity

Alternative strategies

Private equity exposure is material, not marginal.

Even if the percentage differs year to year, the structure is the same:

Limited partnerships

Multi-year lockups

Capital calls and distributions

Layered fee structures

👉 Verification path

MTRS investment allocation tables

PRIM investment disclosures

Annual investment performance summaries

You can see where money is allocated — not how deeply it’s layered.

2.6 — Step five: gross returns (again, not the problem)
As with police funds:

Gross performance is reported

Benchmarks are applied

Numbers look precise and professional

Teachers are often told:

“The system earned X% this year.”

That statement is not false.

But it is incomplete.

2.7 — Step six: net returns become estimates (same problem, bigger scale)
Here the exact same blind spot reappears, but amplified:

Private equity fees are complex

Carried interest depends on exits years later

Interim net returns rely on estimates

Because MTRS is so large:

Small estimation errors scale up fast

Delayed corrections affect funding assumptions statewide

Net numbers today may:

Change quietly later

Never be fully reconciled publicly

Be “good enough” for compliance, but not verification

👉 Verification path

Consultant quarterly reports

Fee and expense disclosures (often summarized)

Board materials (often high-level)

This is where clarity thins out.

2.8 — Step seven: actuaries repeat the same dependency
Actuaries for MTRS:

Use net returns provided

Apply long-term assumptions

Set contribution requirements

They do not:

Audit private fund cash flows

Deconstruct fund-of-fund fees

Independently price illiquid assets

If estimates persist:

Risks roll forward

Errors compound

Accountability diffuses

Same math. Same dependency.

2.9 — Step eight: PERAC oversight (same boundary)
PERAC oversees MTRS just as it does city systems.

PERAC checks:

Filings

Procedures

Compliance with Chapter 32

PERAC does not:

Reconstruct PRIM’s underlying investments

Independently audit private equity valuations

Guarantee that long-term net numbers converge to reality

Again: form vs substance.

2.10 — What teachers actually see
A Springfield teacher typically sees:

A funded ratio

An annual return percentage

Reassurances about long-term stability

They do not see:

Which private funds drive returns

How many fee layers exist

Whether estimates were later revised

How much opacity is structural vs temporary

This is not negligence by teachers.
It is a design choice.

2.11 — The blind spot, stated plainly
For teachers, the blind spot is:

When a statewide pooled system combines private, illiquid investments with estimated net reporting and no mandatory, public, time-bound reconciliation — members cannot independently confirm long-term accuracy.

Same blind spot as police.
Just farther away.

2.12 — Key comparison to Section 1 (why this matters)
Springfield Police

Smaller system

City-level board

Slightly more local visibility

Same private equity opacity

Springfield Teachers

Statewide pooled system

Extra governance layers

Less local visibility

Same private equity opacity

Different routes.
Same dead end.

Why Section 2 matters
This confirms something important:

The problem is structural, not personal.
It does not depend on the honesty of any one board, consultant, or regulator.

The same blind spot appears twice, in two different systems, governed by the same law.

SECTION 3 — Turnpike & Highway Workers: When the Employer Changes but the Blind Spot Doesn’t
(This section covers MassDOT / Highway / Turnpike workers and shows why “state employee” does not mean “more transparent.”)

3.1 — Who we’re talking about (names matter)
Group:

Massachusetts Turnpike Authority workers (historical)

MassDOT / Highway Department employees

Certain transportation, maintenance, and operations staff

Retirement System:

State Employees’ Retirement System (SERS / MSERS)

Governing Law:

Massachusetts Chapter 32

Regulator:

PERAC

Key distinction from Sections 1 & 2:
These workers are state employees, not city or school-district employees.

Many people assume this means:

“The state watches it more closely.”

That assumption is where this section starts to matter.

3.2 — Step one: money leaves the paycheck (still the same)
For a highway or turnpike worker:

Mandatory payroll contribution (rate depends on hire date)

Automatically withheld

Governed by statute, not choice

At the same time:

The Commonwealth contributes as employer

Amount set through actuarial funding schedules

Paid through the state budget

👉 Verification path

Employee pay stubs

State payroll documentation

MSERS contribution schedules

Up to this point, nothing is unusual.

3.3 — Step two: money enters MSERS (bigger pool, less visibility)
Unlike Springfield Police (city)
and unlike Teachers (separate statewide system):

Highway workers’ money goes into MSERS, which includes:

State police (some categories)

Executive branch employees

Transportation workers

Clerical and administrative staff

Various state agencies

This creates:

A very large pooled fund

Many groups with different job risks

Shared investment outcomes

At this point:

Individual worker identity is completely abstracted

Oversight becomes systemic, not personal

3.4 — Step three: investment authority is centralized
MSERS investments are not handled internally by each agency.

They flow through:

PRIM (Pension Reserves Investment Management Board)

External investment managers

Consultants

Custodians

Fund administrators

So the chain is now:
Worker → MSERS → PRIM → Managers → Funds → Sub-funds

This is the longest chain so far.

3.5 — Step four: asset allocation (looks familiar by now)
MSERS asset mix includes:

Public equities

Fixed income

Real estate

Private equity

Hedge funds / alternatives

Opportunistic strategies

The categories look clean on paper.

But private equity again introduces:

Long lockups

Capital calls

Delayed distributions

Multi-layer fee structures

👉 Verification path

PRIM annual report

MSERS investment summaries

Composite asset allocation tables

What’s missing is not allocation — it’s traceability.

3.6 — Step five: gross returns are reported confidently
As with teachers and police:

Annual gross returns are published

Benchmarks are cited

Long-term averages look reassuring

Statements like:

“The system earned X% over Y years”

are technically correct.

But still incomplete.

3.7 — Step six: net returns rely on estimates (same flaw, largest scale yet)
Here the blind spot grows again.

For MSERS:

Private equity net returns are estimated

Fees are complex and uneven

Carried interest may not be settled for years

Interim valuations are model-based

Because the pool is so large:

Small estimation errors → big dollar impacts

Corrections may appear years later

Most members never see the revisions

This is not fraud.
It is structural opacity.

3.8 — Step seven: actuarial assumptions stack on top of estimates
Actuaries:

Use reported net returns

Apply long-term return assumptions

Determine funding schedules

Shape state budget obligations

They do not:

Re-audit underlying private funds

Independently value illiquid assets

Disassemble fund-of-fund structures

So actuarial certainty rests on:

“Best available numbers,” not verified ones.

Same pattern. Bigger consequences.

3.9 — Step eight: PERAC oversight (still procedural)
PERAC oversees MSERS just like the others.

PERAC checks:

Compliance with Chapter 32

Filing completeness

Governance procedures

Audit processes

PERAC does not:

Audit PRIM’s private equity valuations

Force public reconciliation of estimated vs final returns

Require member-level fee transparency

Again:
Oversight exists — but it stops at structure.

3.10 — What highway workers actually see
A MassDOT or turnpike worker typically sees:

Funded ratio

Annual return headline

Assurance of long-term sustainability

They do not see:

Which private funds their money is in

How many layers of fees exist

Whether net returns were revised years later

How much uncertainty exists inside the numbers

They are told to trust the system.

3.11 — The blind spot, restated in plain language
For highway and turnpike workers:

When a massive statewide pension pool relies on estimated net returns from illiquid private investments, members cannot independently verify whether reported performance accurately reflects real, realized outcomes.

Same blind spot.
Largest scale so far.

3.12 — Comparison so far (pattern check)
Springfield Police:
Local board → PE opacity

Springfield Teachers:
Statewide system → PE opacity

Highway / Turnpike Workers:
Massive pooled state system → PE opacity

Different employers.
Different boards.
Same investment structure.
Same visibility loss.

That matters.

Why Section 3 matters
At this point, it’s clear:

This is not about cities vs the state.
It’s not about teachers vs cops vs highway workers.
It’s about how private, illiquid investments behave inside public systems.

The system works — until you ask it to explain itself.

SECTION 4 — Union Workers Outside Chapter 32: Same Blind Spot, Fewer Safeguards
(This section covers federal unions, trade unions, and private-sector union plans — and why the problem doesn’t disappear when PERAC isn’t involved.)

4.1 — Who we’re talking about (this is not PERAC)
This group includes workers such as:

Electricians (IBEW)

Plumbers & pipefitters

Laborers

Carpenters

Federal union employees

Multi-employer pension plan participants

Key difference from Sections 1–3:
These workers are not governed by Massachusetts Chapter 32 and not overseen by PERAC.

Instead, they fall under:

ERISA (Employee Retirement Income Security Act)

Department of Labor (DOL)

PBGC (Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation)

Union-appointed trustees

Many people assume this means:

“More rules = safer money.”

That assumption is shaky.

4.2 — Step one: money leaves the paycheck (still mandatory)
Just like public workers:

Contributions are mandatory

Set by collective bargaining agreements

Withheld automatically

Employer contributions are required

At this stage:

The system feels transparent

Workers often know the contribution rate

Statements appear regular and professional

So far, everything looks better than public systems.

4.3 — Step two: money enters a multi-employer trust
Instead of a city or state retirement board:

Money flows into a union pension trust

Governed by a board of trustees

Trustees typically include:

Union representatives

Employer representatives

Sometimes independent advisors

Here’s the first subtle shift:

Trustees are often not financial experts

Fiduciary duty exists, but technical understanding varies

Decisions rely heavily on consultants

4.4 — Step three: investment authority is outsourced fast
Union pension trusts almost immediately rely on:

Investment consultants

OCIO models

External asset managers

Custodians

Fund administrators

Sound familiar?

Because it is.

This is the same architecture used by:

PERAC-regulated systems

PRIM

MSERS

Teachers’ systems

Different law.
Same machinery.

4.5 — Step four: private equity enters quietly
Most union pension plans now allocate to:

Private equity

Private credit

Infrastructure

Real estate partnerships

Fund-of-funds

Why?
Because consultants tell trustees:

“You need higher returns to stay solvent.”

No vote by members.
No direct consent.
Usually no meaningful explanation.

4.6 — Step five: gross returns are emphasized (again)
Union members are shown:

Plan funded percentage

Average annual returns

“Recovery” narratives after market downturns

Just like public workers:

Gross performance looks healthy

Benchmarks are highlighted

Long-term projections look stable

What’s missing:

Verified net performance

Fee transparency

Valuation uncertainty disclosures

4.7 — Step six: net returns are still estimates (ERISA allows this)
Here’s a critical point many people don’t know:

ERISA does NOT require

Line-item private equity fee disclosure to members

Fund-level valuation audits for each underlying vehicle

Clear reconciliation of estimated vs realized returns

So:

Net returns are often modeled

Fees are embedded

Carried interest may not be visible for years

Legally acceptable
But informationally weak

4.8 — Step seven: trustees rely on consultants (not audits)
Union trustees typically:

Review consultant reports

Approve asset allocation

Rely on summaries

They usually do not:

Audit private fund valuations

Independently test fee calculations

Disassemble fund-of-fund structures

This isn’t corruption.
It’s delegated trust.

4.9 — Step eight: oversight exists, but it’s reactive
ERISA oversight happens when:

A plan becomes distressed

A whistleblower comes forward

The PBGC intervenes

A lawsuit is filed

Unlike PERAC:

There is no routine public audit equivalent

No centralized reporting portal like PROSPER

No annual public system-wide review

Oversight happens after damage, not before.

4.10 — What union members actually see
Most union workers receive:

Annual benefit statements

Estimated retirement payouts

Funded status percentages

They usually do not receive:

A list of private equity funds

Fee breakdowns

Net vs gross reconciliations

Explanations of valuation risk

They’re expected to trust:

Trustees

Consultants

The brand names involved

4.11 — The blind spot (same problem, fewer checks)
For union workers outside Chapter 32:

Private equity and alternative investments introduce layers of opacity where net performance, fees, and valuations are estimated, delayed, or inaccessible — and no regulator proactively forces clarity.

Different regulator.
Same result.

4.12 — Why this section matters
This comparison proves something important:

The blind spot is not a Massachusetts problem

It’s not a PERAC-only problem

It’s not a public vs private problem

It’s a structural pension finance problem.

Wherever:

Illiquid assets exist

Fees are complex

Valuations are estimated

Members are removed from decision-making

The same gap appears.

Pattern so far (Sections 1–4)
Group	Oversight Body	Blind Spot Exists?
Springfield Police	PERAC	Yes
Springfield Teachers	PERAC	Yes
Highway / Turnpike	PERAC + PRIM	Yes
Union / Federal	ERISA / DOL	Yes
Different laws.
Same outcome.

SECTION 5 — Where Net vs. Gross Actually Breaks the System
(This is the section where everything that “looks fine” on paper quietly stops being true.)

5.1 — Start with the simple version people are told
Most workers—police, teachers, highway workers, union members—are taught this mental model:

Gross return = how well investments performed

Net return = what’s left after fees

Fees matter, but “professionals handle that”

Long-term averages smooth everything out

This sounds reasonable.
It’s also incomplete.

5.2 — What gross returns really measure (and don’t)
Gross performance answers one narrow question:

“How did the assets perform before costs, friction, and reality?”

Gross returns:

Are easy to calculate

Are comparable across funds

Are favored by consultants

Look great in presentations

Gross returns do not tell you:

What investors actually earned

Whether fees are compounding against you

Whether returns are realizable or theoretical

Whether valuations reflect market reality

Gross ≠ money in your pocket.

5.3 — Why net returns matter more than anyone admits
Net returns are what fund beneficiaries live on.

But net returns:

Depend on fee accuracy

Depend on timing

Depend on valuation assumptions

Change years later

In public and union systems:

Net returns are often estimated

Fees are embedded, not itemized

Carry is invisible until exit

Revisions happen quietly

So when someone says:

“The fund returned 8% annualized”

The honest follow-up is:

“When measured, verified, and for whom?”

5.4 — Private equity changes the math completely
Once private equity enters the picture:

Assets are illiquid

Valuations are not market-based

Fees are layered

Returns are backdated

Performance is “smoothed”

This is not illegal.
But it breaks intuitive accounting.

5.5 — The valuation lag problem (the hidden gap)
Private funds:

Report values quarterly or annually

Use internal models

Adjust past numbers later

That means:

2021 numbers may change in 2023

2023 numbers may change in 2026

“Strong performance” can reverse

By the time reality shows up:

Trustees have moved on

Members already trusted the figures

Decisions are locked in

5.6 — Why “estimated net returns” are dangerous long-term
Short-term estimates are fine if:

They’re flagged clearly

They’re reconciled later

Errors are corrected publicly

The problem:

Estimates become permanent

Corrections are buried

No one reconciles the full lifecycle

Over 10–20 years:

Small estimation errors compound

Fees quietly erode value

Funding assumptions drift

No single scandal.
Just slow damage.

5.7 — Fee stacking: how money leaks without anyone stealing
In private equity and alternatives, fees stack like this:

Fund-level management fees

Performance fees (carry)

Fund-of-funds fees

Advisor fees

Custodial and admin costs

Each layer may be “reasonable.”
Together, they’re opaque.

Most members never see:

Total effective fee rate

Lifetime fee impact

Fee drag vs public markets

They’re told:

“This is necessary for diversification.”

5.8 — Why audits don’t catch this easily
Audits typically verify:

Whether reports were filed

Whether processes exist

Whether rules were followed procedurally

They usually do not:

Recalculate private valuations

Independently verify carry

Stress-test assumptions

Reconstruct net performance over decades

So audits can be “clean”
while the numbers are still wrong.

5.9 — Consultants unintentionally reinforce the problem
Consultants:

Recommend asset allocation

Select managers

Provide performance summaries

They rarely:

Audit fees

Verify valuations independently

Take responsibility for net accuracy

Why?
Because that’s not their contracted role.

Everyone is doing their job—
just not the missing job.

5.10 — What members think net vs gross means (and why it’s wrong)
Most members believe:

Net = exact

Gross = marketing

Audits ensure accuracy

Reality:

Net is often provisional

Gross dominates decisions

Audits ensure compliance, not truth

This mismatch is the core blind spot.

5.11 — The breaking point: assumptions become policy
Once assumptions are baked into:

Funding schedules

COLA decisions

Contribution rates

Political budgets

Correcting errors becomes painful.

So systems prefer:

Stability over accuracy

Delay over correction

Silence over revision

Again: not malicious—structural.

5.12 — Why this section matters
This is where the system stops being:

“Hard to understand”

And becomes:

“Impossible to verify without help”

If net numbers can’t be reconstructed:

Members can’t self-audit

Trustees can’t truly oversee

Regulators can’t see long-term drift

And trust replaces verification.

What we now know (Sections 1–5)
Money starts transparently

Oversight exists

Professionals are involved

Reports are produced

Audits occur

And yet:

Net truth degrades over time

Fees blur reality

Valuations lag

Corrections disappear

That’s the break.

SECTION 6 — Who Is Supposed to Catch This (and Why They Usually Don’t)
(This is the section where people expect a villain—and instead find a gap.)

6.1 — The question everyone asks
When something feels off, people instinctively ask:

“Isn’t someone supposed to be watching this?”

The uncomfortable answer is: yes — but not in the way people think.

Oversight exists.
Accountability exists.
What’s missing is end-to-end responsibility.

6.2 — The retirement board (local level)
Who they are
For Springfield police, teachers, city workers, etc., the local retirement board is the front door.

They typically include:

Member representatives (workers or retirees)

Employer representatives (city or department)

An appointed chair

An administrator/executive director

What they are responsible for
Hiring consultants

Approving investment strategy

Reviewing reports

Voting on managers

Submitting filings

What they are not equipped to do
Recalculate private equity fees

Audit fund-level valuations

Reverse-engineer net performance

Forensically test assumptions

They rely on others by design.

6.3 — Investment consultants (the guides, not the police)
What consultants do
Recommend asset allocation

Select managers

Produce performance reports

Compare peers

Explain markets to boards

They are influential.
They are smart.
They are not auditors.

What consultants explicitly do not do
Verify fee accuracy

Independently audit valuations

Certify net performance

Guarantee long-term correctness

Most contracts say this plainly.

They guide decisions — they don’t certify truth.

6.4 — Investment managers (the source of the data)
Private equity, real estate, hedge funds, and alternatives:

Generate their own valuations

Report performance internally

Provide estimates before exits

Revise numbers later

They are bound by:

Accounting standards

Disclosure rules

Contracts

They are not required to:

Mark to market daily

Reveal proprietary models

Disclose full internal fee mechanics publicly

This is legal.
It’s also opaque.

6.5 — Auditors (compliance, not reconstruction)
What auditors actually check
Were reports submitted?

Were procedures followed?

Are records consistent internally?

Are controls documented?

What auditors usually do not do
Reprice private assets

Recalculate carried interest

Rebuild 10–20 years of net returns

Test alternative assumptions

Audits confirm process integrity, not outcome accuracy.

So an audit can pass
even if the numbers are soft.

6.6 — PERAC (the regulator)
PERAC:

Oversees 104 retirement systems

Enforces Chapter 32 compliance

Requires filings

Conducts audits

Issues guidance and memos

PERAC ensures:

Rules are followed

Systems file on time

Governance exists

PERAC does not:

Manage money

Select investments

Recalculate fund valuations

Reconstruct fee history

Oversight ≠ ownership.

6.7 — Actuaries (the long-range modelers)
Actuaries:

Use reported data

Project liabilities

Set funding schedules

Model future assumptions

They rely on:

Reported returns

Accepted valuations

Assumed rates

They don’t investigate whether inputs were perfect.
They assume reasonable accuracy.

If inputs drift, outputs drift.

6.8 — Unions (advocates, not auditors)
Unions:

Negotiate benefits

Defend members’ rights

Appoint board members

Advocate politically

They typically do not:

Audit investments

Verify fees

Analyze private equity mechanics

They trust the system like members do —
unless something obviously breaks.

6.9 — State auditors & inspectors
These offices:

Investigate fraud

Examine compliance

Audit agencies

They are usually reactive, not continuous.
They look for:

Misconduct

Waste

Abuse

They are not designed to:

Continuously monitor investment accuracy

Rebuild historical performance

Police valuation models

6.10 — The missing role: lifecycle verifier
Here’s the core issue:

No single entity is responsible for verifying net truth across the full lifecycle of investments.

Everyone touches a piece.
No one owns the whole.

So:

Errors don’t trigger alarms

Estimates harden into fact

Corrections fade into footnotes

6.11 — Why this persists without conspiracy
This isn’t about people being bad.
It’s about systems being fragmented.

Each role says, truthfully:

“That’s not our scope.”

And they’re right.

But the result is:

No one confirms the final answer

Members assume someone did

Confidence replaces verification

6.12 — Why members feel powerless
Members:

Don’t have direct access

Don’t know who to ask

Are told “it’s complicated”

Are shown summaries, not sources

So when something feels wrong, there’s nowhere obvious to go.

That’s the blind spot.

Where we stand after Section 6
We now know:

Oversight exists

Professionals are involved

Rules are followed

Reports are produced

And yet:

No one certifies long-term net accuracy

No one reconstructs the full picture

No one owns the blind spot

That’s not corruption.
That’s a design gap.

SECTION 7 — Where the Money Becomes Hard to See
(This is where transparency slowly fades—not all at once, but step by step.)

7.1 — The moment clarity starts to blur
Up to this point, most money is still visible:

Contributions are clear

Payroll deductions are clear

Employer payments are clear

Cash entering the system is clear

The blur begins after the money leaves the local system and enters layered investment structures.

Not because anyone is hiding it —
but because of how modern investing works.

7.2 — The first visibility drop: pooled investing
Most retirement systems don’t invest alone.

They pool money into:

Commingled funds

Limited partnerships

Fund-of-funds

Collective investment trusts

Why?

Cost efficiency

Access to opportunities

Risk diversification

But pooling means:

Your dollars are mixed with others

Ownership becomes proportional, not discrete

Reporting becomes averaged

From here on out, you’re seeing shares of outcomes, not line-item receipts.

7.3 — The second drop: private assets vs public markets
Public market assets
Stocks, bonds, ETFs

Daily pricing

Transparent markets

Immediate exits

Private assets
Private equity

Venture capital

Private real estate

Infrastructure

Private credit

Private assets:

Don’t trade daily

Aren’t priced by open markets

Use internal valuation models

Update quarterly (sometimes slower)

This isn’t illegal.
It’s standard.

But it means:

Prices are estimates

Lag is normal

Adjustments happen later

7.4 — The third drop: valuation modeling
Private asset values are based on:

Comparable transactions

Discounted cash flow models

Assumptions about growth, exit timing, and multiples

These models:

Are reviewed

Are governed by accounting standards

Are not independently recalculated by every investor

So when a report says:

“Net IRR: 12.4%”

That number depends on:

Assumptions

Timing

Fees

Exit expectations

It’s a best estimate, not a bank balance.

7.5 — The fourth drop: net vs gross reporting
This is where confusion accelerates.

Gross performance
Before fees

Before carried interest

Before fund expenses

Net performance
After management fees

After performance fees

After expenses

After carried interest (eventually)

Private funds often:

Report gross early

Estimate net

True-up net years later

If exits haven’t happened yet:

Carried interest isn’t finalized

Net returns are provisional

So:

Numbers change

History gets revised

Comparisons get messy

7.6 — The fifth drop: timing mismatches
Different parts of the system move on different clocks:

Payroll: biweekly

Contributions: monthly

Public assets: daily

Private assets: quarterly

Actuarial valuations: annually

Audits: periodic

This means:

Reports don’t line up cleanly

One report may use older data than another

Corrections arrive after decisions were made

Nothing breaks — but precision erodes.

7.7 — The sixth drop: layered fees
Fees don’t appear as one line.

They stack:

Management fees (fund level)

Performance fees / carry

Fund-of-fund fees

Administrative fees

Custodial and reporting fees

Some are:

Netted from returns

Not itemized

Estimated

Disclosed separately

Disclosed later

So members ask:

“How much did fees cost me?”

And the honest answer is:

“It depends on time, structure, and realization.”

That’s not comforting — but it’s accurate.

7.8 — The seventh drop: revisions after the fact
Private investments can revise past numbers when:

Assets are sold

Audits occur

Accounting standards update

Errors are corrected

This means:

Old reports may no longer be “wrong”

But they are no longer “right” either

Without a full restatement trail, members can’t see:

What changed

When

Why

By how much

The past becomes fuzzy.

7.9 — Why this doesn’t trigger alarms
Nothing in this process is automatically alarming because:

Each step is allowed

Each role is following standards

Each report is defensible on its own

The problem isn’t a red flag.
It’s cumulative opacity.

7.10 — Where members lose the thread
By the time money reaches:

Private equity

Fund-of-funds

Long-duration vehicles

Members can no longer:

Trace dollars

Match fees to outcomes

Verify net accuracy independently

Understand revisions without expert help

They’re asked to trust the chain.

7.11 — The door metaphor
Think of it like this:

Every step adds a door:

The first door has glass

The next has frosted glass

The next is wood

The last is locked, but labeled “audited”

Nothing behind the door is necessarily wrong.

But you can’t see it anymore.

7.12 — Why this matters before failure
This isn’t about collapse.
It’s about understanding exposure.

If returns are good:

Blind spots feel harmless

If returns drop:

Blind spots become critical

You don’t want to discover opacity after stress hits.

Where we stand after Section 7
We now understand:

Exactly where visibility fades

Why it fades

That fading is legal and normal

How it compounds over time

Next, we look at the real tension point:

What happens when estimates are treated as facts.
